newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Howard asserts right to change laws on land.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Howard asserts right to change laws on land.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Wednesday he has made no decision on how to deal with confusion over native land title, but asserted his right to change the law if necessary.
"It's a very difficult issue. It can't be left as it is," Howard told a news conference after meeting with leaders from the states and territories.
"We have to try to get a solution that is reasonably acceptable to all the people involved," he said.
Howard said he had had a useful meeting with the state premiers, and would meet early next month with aboriginal leaders, as well as miners and pastoralists.
"I don't think anybody relishes the fact that we have had a lot of confusion arise out of this (High Court) decision," he said.
"I don't criticise the decision...but I also assert the right as the leader of the national government to consider changes to the law which we might think are necessary," he said.
In December, the High Court, Australia's senior tribunal, ruled that traditional Aboriginal ownership of land could co-exist with pastoral leases, the main form of title granted to farmers.
The surprise decision extended a 1992 ruling that allowed Aboriginal people to claim native title to vacant Crown land.
Howard said advice to the government suggested the ruling meant a farmer might have to seek permission from a native title holder to build a dam on his property.
"On the advice available to me at the present time, this decision has the potential to create enormous uncertainty," he said.
Howard said he understood the strength of feeling in the aboriginal community, but the government had an obligation to ensure that uncertainty did not continue longer than necessary.
Asked if any solution would breach the spirit of the Racial Discrimination Act, Howard said: "I wouldn't have thought that we will do anything to breach the spirit of racial harmony."
"(But) if you are asking me for a guarantee that we won't touch existing legislation, I can't give that."
Howard said it was possible that native title holder and pastoral rights could co-exist in some circumstances.

"It entirely depends on how those rights are defined and what type of rights they are," he said. "From a practical point of view pastoralists and Aborigines coexist in many parts of Australia very easily."
The prime minister said he had reached no understanding with the premiers or any other group.
"This is a very difficult issue and at the end of the day everyone may have to give a bit in order to have a compromise in the national interest."
State premiers have urged Howard to pursue a legislative solution to the problem to bring certainty for pastoralists.
Aboriginal leaders were meeting in Cairns in northern Australia on Wednesday to discuss issues flowing from the High Court decision.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission chairman Gatjil Djerrkura said on Tuesday that Aboriginal people believed their common law rights to native title on pastoral leases should not be extinguished, and that the Racial Discrimination Act should not be amended.
